section_title: The Down and Dirty: 2009's Top Charterers
section_path: The Down and Dirty: 2009's Top Charterers
section_path_text: The Down and Dirty: 2009's Top Charterers
text:
With refinery utilizations low and volumes on long‐haul trade routes sapped by a 2 million barrel per day drop in worldwide demand, it comes as no surprise that 2009 saw a marked slowdown of activity in the tanker market. The recently completed year was one in which the tanker market was beset by forces both specific to the industry and completely out of its control. An examination of the changes between total fixtures reported in 2008 and 2009 reveals some of the results of the forces that shaped the tanker market over the past year.
As shown in the chart below, the total number of reported spot market fixtures last year failed to reach the levels achieved in 2008 in all but one of the tanker classes discussed. In total, 8,800 fixtures were captured by the Poten & Partners Fixture Database last year, an almost nine percent decrease from the 9, 587 fixtures captured in 2008.

section_path_text: Chart: 2009 - Top Dirty Charterers - What a Difference a Year Makes!
text:

Second only to the United States in oil consumption, demand for transportation fuels from China's growing middle class has been a factor in worldwide crude oil demand for years. The International Energy Agency expects China's oil demand to continue expanding at a rate of 4.7% in 2010, reaching 8.9 million barrels per day. If demand growth continues along its current trajectory and reaches expected levels of 11.5 million barrels per day by 2015, it could lead to significant increases in ton‐mile demand. For illustrative purposes, assuming that these incremental volumes are sourced from the Arabian Gulf, it could create demand for an additional 80 VLCCs to meet Chinese demand by 2015. In fact, these barrels are likely to be sourced from farther away, resulting in even higher ton‐mile demand.
The Arabian Gulf has accounted for more than 70% of Chinese imports since 2005. The EU's new restrictions on marine fuel burned in port and their effect on spot market rates demonstrate that inconsistent enforcement of regulations can have a significant effect on the bottom line. The rules now being more strictly enforced on a selective basis have been known since 2005, allowing plenty of time for ship owners to meet the new regulations. However, the lack of an effective policing and enforcement methodology led many to believe these regulations would not materialize on a practical basis.
As the debate regarding regulation of greenhouse gas emissions from ships reaches the next stage with the meeting of the MEPC next week, lessons learned from existing regulation are important to keep in mind. Considering the repercussions of the sulfur rules for which the market has had five years' warning, the IMO must carefully consider realistic timelines for its sweeping proposals to limit a wider range of harmful greenhouse gases. It must also clearly mandate uniform enforcement and suitable penalties for non‐compliance.
Without a realistic framework, the efforts of these agencies will likely be in vain. Until such a framework is agreed to and put into force, expect the volatility to continue as pockets of availability for specific fuels may create more complications in an already complex market.

Specially‐crafted clauses have been inserted into charterparties for voyages through the area, as owners naturally seek a premium for taking the risks associated with bringing their vessels into the US Gulf. BP is reported to be painting a worst‐case scenario after being called to Washington for closed‐door briefings for lawmakers this week. There have been calls by some lawmakers to raise the liability limit from the $75 million level set by the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 to as much as $10 billion. Special interest groups have run television ads calling for offshore drilling plans to be amended in light of the spill and the Minerals Management Service, responsible for regulating offshore drilling, has already come under increased scrutiny for its ties to energy companies.
What role the reaction to the BP spill will play in the efforts to pass new energy legislation is not yet fully clear, but it is most likely to slow overall progress on the effort. Efforts by Senators John Kerry, Lindsey Graham, and Joseph Lieberman to craft a compromise version of the energy bill, which had already been complicated by the fight over immigration in recent weeks, is likely to be further slowed by the need to address concerns raised by the spill. Senator Graham, a Republican from South Carolina whose support for the new bill was seen as critical, has called for a pause in consideration of the issue and said that the proposal had "no chance" of passing in the current climate.

Waiting for a report and list of recommendations by a commission appointed by the President could prolong the ban, especially as the political storm surrounding the spill continues to build as mid‐term elections approach. In the midst of a still‐recovering economy and high levels of unemployment, the most potent source of opposition to the moratorium is likely to be its impact on employment in the areas surrounding the Gulf, already hurt by damage the spill has brought to the region's fishing industry.
The moratorium is expected to effect 33 drilling rigs, 22 of which are currently employed in the Gulf of Mexico with the remainder scheduled to work there some time during the next six months. The rippling legal consequences of disrupting contracted deepwater operations in the Gulf could drag on for the foreseeable future. Earlier this week, a publically‐listed operator of offshore support vessels vowed to defend the enforcement of existing contracts in the Gulf of Mexico. The company said it would resist any attempt to declare force majeure as a result of either the Deepwater Horizon spill or the moratorium while raising the possibility of relocating some of its vessels to markets overseas.
The tightening of regulation likely to result from the disaster could make future deepwater exploration in the Gulf of Mexico more expensive, complicating the decision‐making of companies considering long‐term investment. Growing concerns that delayed production and tightened regulations enacted after the disaster could inflate the price of oil in years to come may have already been reflected recently in futures markets. Contracts for oil to be delivered in July 2015 have seen their premium over promptly‐delivered supplies rise from $7.68 per barrel before the explosion to $15.28 per barrel today, as shown in the chart below.

As the company deals with an array of short‐term challenges related to the disastrous oil spill in the U.S. Gulf of Mexico, BP briefly turned its attention to the long‐term this week with the release of its annual Statistical Review. For the 59 th year, BP has provided the energy industry with an overview of up‐to‐date statistics on production and consumption of various energy sources in markets all around the world. This year's report and analysis focuses on the search for lessons in the aftermath of 2009, a tumultuous year for the international economy as well as oil markets worldwide.
According to the 2010 Statistical Review, the first contraction in world trade since the Second World War led to a 1.1 % decline in primary energy consumption last year. As shown in the chart below, 2009 marked the first drop in energy consumption since 1982 and the largest percentage drop since 1980. Defined by BP as including use of oil, natural gas, coal, nuclear and hydro power, primary energy consumption fell in all regions, excluding the Asia‐Pacific and the Middle East. This contrast underscores a theme of last year's report which has only been reinforced by the events since: that the countries outside the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) will increasingly be the drivers of future demand growth.

BP sees global oil consumption as having fallen some 1.2 million barrels per day last year, which is also the largest fall since 1982. Drops in oil demand were not consistent across regions, though, with OECD demand displaying the sharpest decline on record while oil demand in non‐ OECD countries continued to grow, albeit at a slower pace. This disparity helped lead to the second consecutive decline in global oil trade, according to BP, with the United States accounting for the majority of the net decline in imports.
On the supply side, sustained production cuts from the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) last year led to the group's most significant output decline since 1983. These cuts accounted for most of the 2.6% drop in worldwide oil production reported by BP, which occurred despite a slight increase in non‐OPEC production. Production increases in Russia, Brazil, and Azerbaijan contributed to this growth, but the largest source of non‐OPEC supply growth last year was the United States.
The United States increased its oil production by 460 kb/d in 2009, a 7 % increase from the previous year, as shown in the chart below. BP credited developments in the Gulf of Mexico for most of this increase. Recognizing that this may make some uncomfortable in light of recent events in the Gulf, BP reminded that the central importance of such complicated development projects were "a piece of the reality in which we all live."

On the back of the shipping boom during 2004 to 2008, publically‐listed shipping companies gained street credibility and general popularity among retail investors. Tanker industry IPOs issued in 2010 have been met with a mixed initial reception thus far, but could be well positioned to benefit as investors are lured back into the sector by reports of a stronger‐than expected recovery in oil demand.

Investors are wisely focused on the value of underlying assets and are somewhat reluctant to blindly buy into the trade growth fundamentals story. Not surprisingly, those shipowners who are able to get bank loans are facing stricter covenants and higher spreads. A few established public shipping companies, however, have been successful at tapping public markets this year. After threatening to follow a path that some projections showed would send it through the heart of the U.S. Gulf of Mexico, Hurricane Alex weakened into a topical depression which broke up over central Mexico this week. Alex peaked on Wednesday as a Category 2 storm which forced the temporary closure of more than 20 percent of domestic crude oil output and delayed ongoing efforts to clean and contain oil spewing from the nearby Macando well. While the storm seems to have spared the Gulf of Mexico the worst of what was feared for it, Hurricane Alex serves as a warning that the region will likely confront significant weather‐related challenges before the hurricane season reaches its height in September.
Hurricane Alex was the earliest Atlantic hurricane since 1995 and meteorologists are already warning that they expect this year's hurricane season to be a particularly active one. The National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Association (NOAA) forecasts that there is an 85% chance that this year's storm season will be worse than normal. This year's prediction of between 8 and 19 hurricanes is almost double the number of storms predicted in 2007, as shown in the chart below. If their predictions prove accurate, storm conditions may come to play a heightened role in determining both tanker freight rates and the pace of progress in the Deepwater Horizon recovery effort.

While Hurricane Alex did not come into direct contact with the main oil spill region, the storm did force closures of important oil loading ports and production sites this week. The Louisiana Offshore Oil Port was forced to halt offloading operations on June 29 and two of Mexico's main oil ports on the Gulf Coast were also forced to briefly close. Lightering operations at Southwest Pass, the main deepwater entrance to the Mississippi River, were forced to cease along with the closures of the Houston Ship Channel and other ports along the coast of Texas. Operations at most affected ports resumed Thursday.
The U.S. Gulf is home to a significant portion of domestic crude oil production and hurricanes in the region have played a role in sharp decreases in production seen in recent years, as shown in the chart below. Hurricane Alex led to the suspension of about 350 kb/d of domestic crude oil production and the evacuation of six rigs and 69 production platforms in the Gulf of Mexico, according to the US Department of Ocean Energy Management, Regulation and Enforcement. In its short‐term outlook for June, the Energy Information Administration (EIA) said it expects disruptions of up to 26 million barrels of production as a result of this year's hurricane season.

Alongside China, India has emerged as an important driver of many of the trends expected to determine the direction of future oil and tanker markets. Its rapidly‐growing economy has been important in shifting the center of oil demand growth eastward. Additionally, its export refineries have impacted both regional and international refined product trade flows. In a development likely to churn future oil and tanker markets, in late June, India moved to begin phasing out its subsidies for transportation fuels. The decision is an important step for balancing the Indian economy and may eventually provide an example for other countries looking to make similar changes in the years to come.
It is strong economic growth over the past decade which has helped transform India into an important oil consumer and refined product exporter. Strength in India's economy is expected to continue going forward, with 9.4% GDP growth projected for this year according to the updated economic outlook released by the International Monetary Fund earlier this week. Demand for crude oil is also expected to continue its growth; from 2.7 mbd this year to 3.5 mbd by 2014, as shown in the chart below. India's removal of subsidies for gasoline is part of an effort to control the effects of its demand growth and could mark the beginning of an important transition for the entire Indian economy.

One of the most important motivations for the liberalization of gasoline prices in India has been a desire to minimize the economic effects of government subsidies in light of India's recent demand growth. While the Finance Ministry acknowledged that the removal of subsidies would likely bring about an increase in inflation in the near term, the change is also expected to help reduce India's $5.5 billion oil subsidy bill. Fuel subsidies represent about 2.5% of government spending and there is hope that these savings will play an important role in helping India meet its goal of cutting the budget deficit to 5.5% of GDP from almost 7 % last year.
The change is also expected to boost profits at India's state‐owned refiners, who were previously required to charge prices dictated by the government. While India's state‐owned refiners are expected to see more than $20 billion in losses from these subsidies this year alone, the nation's private refiners have been able to shift their focus to international markets. The removal of gasoline subsidies will now allow state‐run refiners to raise the price of gasoline by about seven percent and has inspired plans by private and state refiners alike to expand their distribution networks inside the country.
India's crude oil imports have come predominately from the Arabian Gulf and West Africa, as shown in the graph below, which displays reported spot crude oil volumes into India by major load zone since 2007. As India's refiners are able to capture more profit in domestic markets that enables them to grow to their full potential, they are likely to return some of those proceeds towards securing access to future supplies, an effort in which they have often been outmatched by China in recent years. The Indian government has recently taken several steps to encourage its companies make acquisitions overseas, which could ultimately feed ton‐mile demand growth in the region.

With the enactment of a new U.S. sanctions regime earlier this month, the tanker industry has once again found itself drawn directly into the fray surrounding Iran. On July 1 st , President Obama signed the Comprehensive Iran Sanctions, Accountability, and Divestment Act of 2010, imposing further restrictions on business dealings with Iran. These unilateral sanctions were designed to reinforce a new set of UN sanctions passed in June by attempting to further limit Iran's critical need for refined product imports, highlighted in the chart below. While companies actively engaged in such trades will likely have long suspected such a tightening was forthcoming, the wide‐ranging nature and stiff penalties contained within the recently‐passed law warrant close attention.
The new law reinforces and expands on the 1996 Iran Sanctions Act in ways that bring petroleum transportation and the tanker industry into a sharper focus. Under the new law, oil and liquefied natural gas tankers have been added explicitly to the definition of "petroleum and natural gas resources", investment in and provision of which is prohibited. The new law requires the president to impose sanctions on those that "sell, lease or provide goods, services, technology, information or support that could directly and significantly enhance Iran's ability to import refined products." The new sanctions apply when the fair market value exceeds $1 million for a single transaction or $5 million annually. Critically, the law extends its prohibitions to include shipping services, including insurance, financing and brokerage.

Facing a likely future of tightened environmental regulation and rising marine fuel costs, efforts are underway to standardize efficiency practices in the tanker industry. Chief among these efforts is the "Virtual Arrival" scheme developed by Intertanko and the Oil Companies International Marine Forum (OCIMF). Though not strictly speaking a slow steaming proposal, Virtual Arrival similarly encourages consensus between ship owners and ports on speed and arrival time as a way to alleviate port congestion. The proposal is a step toward formalizing efficiency practices in an industry that is likely to face greenhouse gas emissions regulation some time in the future. However, it is an initiative that will certainly take time to be fully accepted in the market.
Under the Virtual Arrival system, slots at discharge ports are assigned mid‐voyage based on availability and weather conditions, as illustrated below. After destination berths have been assigned, the vessel slows to an agreed‐to speed along a route designed to ensure minimal congestion at the port. Sometimes called "eco‐routing", the system aims to change the way voyage performance is measured, incorporating environmental concerns and recovering earnings lost by full steaming to port, only to wait days to load or discharge.

The Virtual Arrival system was tested in September 2009, when BP Shipping used it on a voyage from Batumi in the Black Sea to the UK Isle of Grain. In March, the Marine Environmental Protection Committee (MEPC) of the IMO met in London to discuss competing proposals for market‐based measures to regulate marine emissions of greenhouse gases. The Virtual Arrival scheme has gathered support partially on the expectation that some market‐ based instrument will be introduced. Proponents highlight that by encouraging a division of fuel and emissions savings between a ship's operator and charterer, the Virtual Arrival system incorporates port authorities and charterers into greenhouse gas regulation, whereas most other proposals have focused responsibility for shipping emissions solely on operators.
Well intentioned as they may be, any attempts to change well‐worn shipping practices during a still‐challenging tanker market are likely to encounter stiff resistance. Environmental efforts such as Virtual Arrival must be widely adopted in order to have a material effect. It is only a select few companies who are in a position to begin preparing now for regulation that may not materialize for years, if ever. Meanwhile, ship owners and charterers will continue to be driven by forces that have long encouraged efficiency‐economics.

Last month, the International Energy Agency (IEA) announced that in 2009, China surpassed the United States to become the world's largest energy consumer. Measured in combined use of crude oil, nuclear, coal, natural gas and other energy sources, China consumed 2.25 billion tons of oil equivalent in 2009, 4% more than the United States. Rather than heralding the beginning of a new era in energy, the announcement merely confirmed what has been clear for some time; China's growth will be a central driver for the international economy in the years to come.
For the tanker market, China has been an increasingly important factor since the early 1990s, when domestic crude oil production began to lag behind the nation's explosive oil demand growth, as shown in the chart below. Going forward, China's ultimate effect on the tanker market will be determined by the interaction of its economic development, oil demand, refining capacity additions, as well its environmental initiatives and ongoing efforts to amass controlled tonnage. These and other factors surrounding the PRC's impact on the tanker market over the next decade will be addressed in Poten & Partners' upcoming multi‐client study, China: Driving Global Commerce and Tanker Trade.

Recent years of offshore crude oil discoveries could put Brazil among the world's largest oil producers while long‐term supply contracts with overseas end users make it a significant source of future ton‐mile demand.
With population growth which has moderated as its economy has continued to develop rapidly, Brazil managed to stabilize the energy intensity of its economy in recent years, as seen in the chart below. text:
Brazil's effort to expand its domestic oil production through the exploration of its offshore resources began decades ago and is starting to make a contribution to its overall energy position. The EIA estimates Brazil's reserves at 12.6 billion barrels, with the majority of supplies located in deep water off its southeastern coast. Apart from producing supplies which will eventually enter international markets, development of these offshore resources has helped turn Brazil into an important market for shuttle tankers.
The most important of Brazil's recent offshore discoveries, the Tupi field located in the offshore Campos Basin, is the largest Western Hemisphere oil discovery in 30 years. Discovered in 2006, Tupi is expected to contain as much as 8 billion barrels of recoverable reserves. In addition, the Jupiter and Cariocoa fields in the region have helped make Brazil an important contributor to growth in non‐OPEC oil production expected in the years to come.
While the country once imported about 80% of its crude oil requirements, Brazil became a net exporter of oil in 2009, when its crude oil production reached an average of just under 2.5 mb/d. With several projects which have come on‐stream in recent years building towards maximum production, the International Energy Agency sees the trend of increasing production continuing this year, with production expected to reach 2.67 mb/d. Its use of hydroelectric power for electricity generation has allowed it to dedicate more of these supplies for export.
While Brazil has long exported its crude oil, its status as a net crude oil exporter is only just starting to be reflected in reported dirty fixture volumes. As shown in the chart below, there have been fifty‐six reported Suezmax fixtures from Brazil so far in 2010, surpassing 2009's total and best reflecting how the upward trend in crude oil exports from Brazil will impact the tanker market. The eight reported VLCC fixtures from Brazil this year, on track to surpass the 12 reported in 2009, also suggest Brazil's potential as a significant source of ton‐mile demand. Not surprisingly, voyages to the U.S. Gulf on Suezmaxes have been the most frequently reported fixtures from Brazil, but as use of its crude oil expands along with production, voyages to more distant markets are expected to take on an increased role in the country's export mix.

In late May, the Interior Department announced a six month moratorium on deepwater drilling in the U.S. Gulf. The action was quickly challenged in court by companies involved in offshore drilling while also being drawn into a political debate which has centered around its effect on regional employment. In mid‐July, the Interior Department was forced to issue a second moratorium after its initial attempt was blocked by a federal judge. The new director of the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management created following the spill has said he hopes to be able to end the deep‐water drilling moratorium before it is scheduled to expire at the end of November. Still, some still fear that incorporating input from the many reviews and reports commissioned immediately following the spill could delay production in the region even longer.
The fact that reductions in domestic crude oil output growth are expected to occur alongside a strengthening in U.S. demand means that they will likely lead to an increase in imports. The specter of vessel deliveries to come and indications of a slower economic recovery have led some to conclude from this vantage point that tanker markets will struggle for the remainder of 2010. A number of factors can lead to a slowdown in the tanker market as August winds to a close. Extended summer vacations in worldwide shipping centers, combined with refinery maintenance and reduced demand for heating oil in Western markets, can contribute to a slowdown in import activity. This increases the supply of vessels seeking employment, typically producing a dip in voyage earnings during the third quarter. The decades to come will see an increasing focus on limiting the environmental impact of worldwide energy demand growth by reducing carbon dioxide (C02) emissions. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has estimated that more than $45 trillion in investment will be required to produce the halving of global CO2 emissions by 2050 called for by some world leaders. While there have been early signs of progress in this proposed "decarbonization" of the global economy, the pace of expected growth dictates that oil and gas will continue to play an integral role in meeting the world's energy demand, even as renewable alternatives are developed. These and other themes were discussed earlier this week at the Japan Society, where head of Poten & Partners' Tanker Department activities, Jeffrey Goetz, moderated a presentation by IEA Executive Director, Nobuo Tanaka.
Mr. Tanaka was appearing at the Japan Society to relay the findings of the IEA's Energy Technology Perspectives report, which contains scenarios for the future development of energy demand and carbon emissions. Released earlier this summer, the report presents a baseline scenario in which energy demand and policy continue along their current path and a BLUE Map scenario which envisions a step‐change reduction in CO2 emissions. These scenarios are not forecasts, but rather an attempt to illustrate changes necessary to meet proposed emissions reduction targets, as summarized in the chart below .

The U.S. trade deficit with China was $227 billion last year and could reach as high as $267 billion this year by some estimates. As shown in the chart below, US imports from China have increasingly outpaced U.S. exports to the country for years, with 2010 on track to continue a trajectory interrupted by the recession of 2009. An appreciation of the Chinese Renminbi is a part of the re‐balancing of the international economy called for by many economists. It is moreover a testament to the country's ever‐growing industrial muscle.
A recent report from the Economic Policy Institute projected that China's currency controls and resulting trade deficit could displace about 540 thousand American jobs this year. On a practical basis, reluctance from China to cooperate with respect to the currency wishes of the West could result in extreme measures such as the U.S. Commerce Department imposing trade sanctions.
The most significant of the retaliatory measures proposed as responses to continued inaction on China's currency would impose tariffs that would have widespread impact of trade of all kinds. Successfully pressuring the Chinese government to sharply raise the value of their currency risks the possibility of social disruption and economic stagnation as was seen in Japan following its rapid re‐valuation of the Yen. Facing these undesirable likely outcomes, this is an issue that is perhaps best framed by the long‐term challenges facing both countries.
The currency valuation dispute highlights China's unique position as a developing country with a de‐facto role as an economic leader. As policymakers in Beijing attempt to balance these demands, it is important to consider that a gradual appreciation of its currency is a step towards a transformation into a more‐domestically‐focused Chinese economy. While it is true that manufacturing jobs in the United States have declined as the U.S. has come to rely on Chinese‐ produced goods, the structural challenges facing the American economy are more complex than China's careful management of its exchange rate.
As a result of China's growing prominence in international oil markets, issues surrounding it's currency valuation could have a significant impact on the tanker business over the years to come. Considering the role China has played in sustaining tanker demand throughout the economic disruptions of recent years and the importance of its continued economic growth for the industry's future, the tanker market would be well served to support China's gradual approach.

Last week industry experts gathered in Miami at the Eden Roc Hotel for the Annual ASBA Cargo Conference. This year's excellent panel of speakers were asked to confront the question of "What's on the Horizon?" Monday morning the conference opened with Jeanne Cardona, 'Executive Director of ASBA,' introducing the Tanker Panel. The topics discussed varied from the process of U.S Flag vessel recycling to the implication of Sanctions on Iran. Following this, the dry cargo panel provided a detailed and experienced insight into the alumina, bauxite and coal trades as well as the likes of James Russell-Walling of 'Eagle Bulk Shipping' and John Wobensmith of the newly formed publicly listed company 'Baltic Trading' presenting an owner's perspective of the market. This concluded a very engaging morning of lectures.
Special mention should, however, be directed towards Ken Applegate, 'Vice President of Transportation at Valero Energy Corporation' who highlighted the conference with an enlightened discussion on the hotly debated topic of the impact of carbon emission proposals on the maritime sector.
Shipping is not explicitly covered by the United Nation's Kyoto Protocol, thus the industry remains largely unregulated. The dance here of course is the contango, which occurs when the spot price of a commodity is lower than the future price. When this structure is in place opportunity knocks to buy now and deliver later and rake in a profit. The rub lies in the availability and cost of storage. Amply supplied crude markets may open opportunity to profit from contango, but they also have resulted in little free space in onshore storage tanks. Last month, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) issued its response to a March 2009 petition from a group of fuel ethanol promoters and producers to allow bringing to market gasoline containing up to 15% ethanol by volume (E15). The response came in the form of a carefully worded waiver and promptly drew howls of complaints from both proponents and opponents of more ethanol blending. The clatter of discontent from both aisles surrounding this issue left some people wondering what exactly was gained by the EPA's expenditure of time and taxpayer money to arrive at the decision.
The EPA's partial waiver allows, but does not require, light‐duty motor vehicles from model year (MY) 2007 and newer to use E15, but does not allow the use of E15 in these vehicles built in MY 2000 and earlier. A decision on the suitability of E15 in vehicles from MY 2001 through MY 2006 was deferred pending the review of data from tests currently being conducted. To reach its partial waiver, the EPA evaluated E15 on four criteria: tailpipe emissions, evaporative emissions, material compatibility, and the ability to drive and operate the vehicles. Not surprisingly, this waiver came with conditions attached. One of these conditions requires that parties involved in the manufacture and sale of E15 submit plans to reduce the potential for mis‐fueling.

One thing parties on both sides of the issue seem to have in common is their displeasure with the waiver. Additionally, opponents voiced concerns that older vehicles and engines in motorcycles, boats and outdoor power equipment might react adversely to E15. In a perfect world, the yet‐to‐be specified EPA conditions to minimize mis‐fueling would, of course, work perfectly. While the relative strengths of the leading world economies will be the ultimate driver of sustained trade growth, it is the relative strength of currencies which are being discussed as potential drivers of the tanker asset market in the near term. Debate surrounding currency pressures have become a topic of increasing significance between the United States and China. Shipbuilding in particular finds itself at the forefront of this entanglement in countries like South Korea, where businesses must regularly manage the inflow of foreign currency with the domestic outflow.
In the United States, the Federal Reserve Bank has set in sight objectives similar to the Chinese by fostering a low interest rate environment and seeking to increase the monetary supply through quantitative easing. text: It's that time of year again! The Worldscale Association has published the new schedule of nominal freight rates for oil tanker trades that will take effect in January 2011. The nominal freight rates, or flat rates, are intended to provide a standard of reference across various voyages for charterers and shipowners trading in the spot tanker market. The Worldscale market rate is merely a percentage of the published flat rate. Its level and volatility reflect the strength and weakness of the market on a daily basis. The chart below shows the change in flat rates for a selection of key tanker trades since 2007. The primary drivers of the change in flat rates are bunker prices and port charges. As can be seen from this chart below, flat rates are on the rise for 2011 by and average of 20% for the trades depicted. On a practical basis, however, the change in flat rate does not have a material effect on the earnings of shipowners and the total cost of freight to charterers as the Worldscale rate will adjusts to keep parity. More than anything else, this annual adjustment means that tanker market participants will have to recalibrate their sense of how much each Worldscale point means on each particular trade in dollars and adjust their commercial expectations accordingly.

As December winds down and the focus of ship owners and charterers shifts towards the coming year's various projected outlooks and forecasts, several common themes will again catch the attention of all shipping market participants. Chief amongst these for owners of vessels operating in the vicinity of the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden is the evolving threat of piracy.
A recent report released by Lloyd's Joint War Committee notes that since the upsurge in piracy‐ related activities in 2008, the threat of piracy has evolved just as materially as the practices and strategies implemented to prevent it. Notably, the committee addresses the issue of the increased effective range of Somali‐based piracy utilizing previously‐captured vessels as 'mother ships' from which the attacks originate. The course of action taken by the committee was to expand the existing areas it deems commercial vessels to be 'at risk' of attack as 2010 saw numerous attacks occur outside the previously designated risk area.
The Joint War Committee represents the interests of those writing war risks in the London markets. Its decision to expand the stretch of waterways deemed at elevated risk of piracy threat will mean higher operating costs for owners as they are faced with the threat of attack further out at sea. Specifically, ships transiting the Western Indian Ocean will be faced with premium piracy 'riders' to reflect the risk they undertake transiting the area. A quick overview of the increasing frequency of the attacks (in addition to their being staged further offshore) makes it easy to understand why insurers will be charging more to absorb the greater cost of mounting insurance claims.

Existing efforts to thwart the growing piracy problem have been met with mixed results. Multinational task forces assembled in the region operating as part of the Combined Maritime Forces under the US 5 th Fleet have had limited success in dealing with the growing threat. The geographic area over which the attacks are occurring seems to have grown too broad in size for international counter‐piracy forces to constantly monitor with any degree of great effectiveness. Somalia has been mulling the idea of hiring a private military security contractor to train and deploy a 1,000 man antipiracy force in the capital of Mogadishu. The force would be funded by an unidentified country according to media reports, and spearheaded by the security company Saracen International. Saracen's operations would seek to eliminate pirate threats "on land" through the establishment of a trained security force led in part by a former US Ambassador and CIA officials. The establishment of private security forces draws concerns from all corners of the international community, however, particularly when funding for such projects is being supplied by unidentified countries - even if it is for sake of avoiding terrorist retribution as claimed.
The growing piracy threat, on both a numeric and geographic basis, is testing the limits of the current preventative measures taken by the international community. Decisions such as those noted above by the Joint War Committee will result in higher costs to ship owners and ultimately consumers putting pressure on end users and ship owners alike to find solutions. Should the attacks continue to occur and expand with the impunity and scope witnessed in the past several years, it can be concluded that attitudes toward arming merchant ships may continue to evolve as well.

text: As 2010 comes to a close, a broad overview of equity markets leads many to believe an economic recovery from the lows experienced in 2008 is at hand. Debate as to whether the market is a leading or lagging indicator of real economic growth aside, the positive returns in the major indices cannot be ignored. Year to date gains of 9.8% 12.8% and 16.1% in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, Standard and Poor's 500, and Nasdaq, respectively, all bear testament to a stock market continuing to rebound from the troughs of the financial crisis. These gains however must be viewed in the context of current monetary policy, rising commodities prices, and a host of data to be truly relevant to the casual observer. As the graph below demonstrates, ship owners and tanker market participants may be wise to look closer to home in their own sector for clues as to whether the rebound in equities is truly indicative of a world economy on the mend.

The "burden of proof of solvency" ping‐ponged through European sovereign debt markets bringing a level of volatility, the likes and scope of which the world had not seen, to the currency markets. The United States Federal Reserve played its own part in the ongoing saga with the announcement of additional quantitative easing in efforts to help sustain the fragile economic recovery at hand. Stimulus events had an undeniably positive impact on equity and commodity markets as both rallied with each successive stimulus announcement. These events however, stood in stark contrast to the palpable fear that gripped investors the afternoon of May 6 th as the "Flash Crash" jarred bullish sentiment in the wake of a 1014 point decline in the DOW in a matter of moments. Amidst the continued commotion that characterized the economic climate of 2010 however, tanker rates remained subdued.
Given the multitude of factors affecting market sentiment it can be easy to get lost in every manner of analysis, news‐reporting and asset‐class correlation. However, a closer look at tanker earnings reveals an interesting relationship with equity markets as well as domestic economic growth. Looking at a ten year chart of VLCC earnings against the S&P500 index and the U.S. Gross Domestic Product, we can evaluate just how shipping earnings stacked up against equity performance and economic growth rates. By no means perfectly correlated, it is still clear to see the strong similarities between the different markets.

Lending further credence to shipping rates' forward indication of economic recovery, a look at earnings versus GDP paints a somewhat compelling picture. Tanker earnings anticipated the steepening curve (accelerated growth) of GDP from 2002 through 2005 and responded notching highs for the decade in mid 2004. As tanker earnings fell for the next several years, the flattening of the GDP curve indicated a deceleration of GDP growth in conjunction. Remarkably, tanker earnings plummeted at nearly the same time the United States experienced a GDP decline in 2008 in what can only be described as the most striking correlation between GDP and tanker earnings in the last decade.
Looking ahead, one would be hard‐pressed to explain to most tanker owners that the equity markets are painting a picture of healthy economic growth at a time when rates remain comparatively low on a historical basis. The data implied by the charts can lead to the assumption that GDP growth (and acceleration) is anticipated in the form of rising tanker earnings.
